Our research analyzed the production of charged particles in high-energy collisions
resulting from new extra-dimension scenarios in the EPOS LHC generator. Collisions
examined ranged from the lowest ($96$ pb$^{-1}$ in $0.197$ GeV nucleon-nucleon collisions
at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 0.89$ GeV to 80 pb$^{-1}$ in 38 TeV nucleon-nucleon collisions
at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV. Calculations based on the EPOS LHC generator
matched observations of particle ratios in mid-to-large collision systems at lower
transverse momentum. System-size dependencies in EPOS LHC collisions were confirmed
by the absence of significant collective phenomena and differences in charged particle
production in collisions of varying system sizes.

The complex interconnectivity of urban infrastructure, which can be understood using graph theory, has a significant impact on how cities function and respond to crises. We propose a new method for analyzing the stability of cities in the face of social unrest using mathematical models. By applying this method to the example of post-election protests in Kinshasa, we used geospatial data to create maps of the city's infrastructure and model how different neighborhoods interacted with each other. These models helped us better understand the interplay between the distribution of resources, the movement of people, and the spread of unrest, revealing how the physical layout of the city influenced the course of events. We found that a particular configuration of the city's infrastructure created a tipping point that contributed to the escalation of the crisis. We also found that the introduction of food aid had a limited impact on reducing unrest in some areas, while in other areas it had no effect, and could even have a negative impact in some cases.

This paper introduces a new Brzozowski derivative operator for regular expressions based on the star height, which we call S\*. The key property of this operator is that it adheres to a specific syntax, allowing it to efficiently determine if one regular expression is contained within another through a symbolic approach.

This paper conducts a comprehensive survey of Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) methods
that utilize both visual and inertial sensors for state estimation. We divide VIO
methods into three categories based on their implementation details and provide
an in-depth examination of their algorithms, constraints, and limitations. We also
compare and contrast various deep learning-based VIO and monocular VIO methods,
discussing potential future research directions in this field. We conclude by
evaluating the future challenges and potential applications of VIO in different
scenarios.

Our analysis classifies all possible topological phenomena in three-dimensional systems, expanding on previous work by categorizing higher-order Weyl materials as both source and sink of novel topology, which we call "square-root topology." We demonstrate that all vacua can be connected to each other through paths of higher-order Weyl points, establishing a comprehensive framework that integrates both the pair and triplet topological insulator categories. This framework is underpinned by the Weyl's theorem of continued fractions and is reflected in the classification of three-dimensional topological systems through the Weyl's theorem of continued fractions and the Fu-Kane indicator, which together provide a comprehensive roadmap for identifying square-root topology and the associated robust surface and Robust bulk states in materials.

This study investigates how different edge finite element methods resolve data completion problems, particularly with regard to reconstructing missing boundary data in the Dirichlet problem for the Laplace equation. Various edge finite element methods are examined, including their ability to accurately recover boundary values from incomplete data, as measured by the error in the $H^1$ norm. Key findings demonstrate that the optimal choice of elements can significantly reduce the error by approximately two orders of magnitude, when compared to other methods, such as continuous or discontinuous Galerkin elements. A key contribution of this research is the derivation of a priori error estimates for the edge finite element method, which provide a stronger convergence rate than previously established results. A series of numerical experiments are also presented to complement these theoretical findings.

In the context of a student model being trained to match a teacher model using knowledge amalgamation, a novel method is proposed that utilizes a saliency-based approach. The approach takes knowledge reuse methods, such as knowledge distillation or masked language modeling, and identifies the most crucial data points that the model needs to master. The proposed method incorporates a regularization term into the loss function to ensure the model's accuracy on these high-priority data points. The data points are then filtered out of the training set to create a new, smaller dataset for the model to be trained on. The proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness in knowledge amalgamation by achieving comparable performance to the original model while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources required. The method also allows for additional modifications, such as using pre-trained models and incorporating multiple models. The proposed approach is applicable to a wide range of models and datasets, including large language models like BERT and CLIP.

We examine the number of quartic extensions of a base number field $k$ with degree 4 under the Galois group S4, where a specific quartic elliptic curve defined over the field extensions does not gain rank compared to the base field. We establish an upper limit on the number of such extensions and demonstrate multiple instances across various base fields, including rational numbers, imaginary quadratic fields, and real quadratic fields.

We've conducted a comprehensive analysis of the irreversible entropy generated through a quantum system's interaction with its surroundings as the system undergoes a quantum quench. This research applies an approximate hydrodynamic approach, considering both stochastic heating and dissipation, to investigate the entropic consequences of quenching. We derived precise expressions to calculate changes in the system's entropy and temperature, using a linear response theory framework. These results allow us to examine the interplay between heating, dissipation, and non-equilibrium dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that the entropy change can be expressed in terms of the initial state, the surrounding environment, and the quench parameter. Furthermore, we found that the final temperature exhibits non-monotonic behavior, resulting from the interplay between heating and dissipation. Our research reveals that the total irreversibility can be decomposed into contributions from heating, dissipation, and the system's initial state. This work also highlights the importance of considering multi-parameter responses, demonstrating that the entropic consequences of quenching depend on multiple parameters, including the quench amplitude and duration. Our approach applies to various quantum systems, including both discrete and continuous systems described by either the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian or the XY Hamiltonian.

Quantifying non-unitary dynamics through the time it takes for a system to become indistinguishable from its initial state is a recent idea. This approach can be framed as a problem of minimizing the time it takes for a system to become indistinguishable from an initial state generated by a specific non-unitary process. Our study determines the minimum time required for a system to become indistinguishable from its initial state in non-unitary dynamics, under the assumption of a specific system and environment configuration. It shows that the distinguishability time is bounded below by the system's largest Liouville time-scale, the system's smallest decay time-scale, and the minimum time-scale associated with the system's decay channels. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the time-scales at which the system's properties change are interlinked with the coefficients of the system's Hamiltonian, coupling operators, and their corresponding decay channels. Our analysis also reveals that the time-scales at which the system's properties change are non-monotonic and depend on both the system and environment parameters.

Consider a set of points within an $n$-dimensional unit cube, denoted as $Q_n$. Given these points, we seek to establish the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex formed by a subset of these points, with the number of points in this subset equal to $n+1$. Our main theorem provides an insufficient number of points below which we cannot guarantee the existence of such a simplex within the unit cube, while all points are less than $e^{n^2}$, up to a factor of $n$. This result improves upon a previous bound established by Erdélyi in 1992. Additionally, our proof techniques yield a more general result, showing that we can form a nondegenerate regular simplex using $n+1$ points from any convex shape with a certain geometric property, as long as the number of points within the shape is sufficiently large.

This research investigates the differences in near-surface carrier concentrations for silicon wafers subjected to different oxidation processes. Initially, the carrier concentrations were measured for etched buffer oxide silicon and compared to those for etched silicon alone. The results showed significantly higher carrier concentrations for the etched silicon, with values ranging from 1x10^17 to 1.5x10^18 per cubic meter. To further analyze the data, the carrier concentrations were modeled using a derivative of the Fermi-Dirac equation, taking into account the thickness of the oxide layer and the charge in the space charge region. The calculated charges agreed with the measured carrier concentrations to within a few percent, providing a precise understanding of the charge in the space charge region and allowing for calculation of the carrier concentrations in the silicon substrate. This calculation revealed that the carrier concentrations in the silicon substrate ranged from 5x10^16 to 1x10^17 per cubic meter, indicating a decrease with increasing oxidation temperature.

The exchange of mass and energy between a planet's surface, core, atmosphere, and magnetosphere/ionsosphere can significantly impact the atmospheric evolution of close-in planets over time. This interior-exterior cycling exchange may have a major effect on the atmospheric composition of these planets, potentially leading to the stabilization of their climate and influencing the rate of atmospheric escape. Although existing research primarily focuses on the short-term effects of this exchange, its long-term consequences are more complex and vary greatly depending on several factors, including the planets' orbital periods, core heat budgets, and the extent of atmospheric interaction with the magnetosphere/ionspheres. Mathematical modeling reveals that the evolution of a planet's atmosphere is highly non-linear over time, with periods of rapid atmospheric loss giving way to prolonged periods of stable atmospheric retention. The eventual outcome for these planets is either complete atmospheric loss or retention of their atmospheres. The model's predictions are consistent with observations of close-in planets with maintained atmospheres or without atmospheres.

This research introduces the nonlinear Hawkes process, expanding on the linear Hawkes model to capture complex interactions within a collection of point processes. By incorporating non-linear response to incoming events, the nonlinear Hawkes model offers a flexible framework that can be applied to a variety of situations, where processes interact and influence one another, such as computer networks, population dynamics, and financial transactions. We have derived an efficient algorithm for maximum likelihood parameter estimation and proven that the nonlinear Hawkes process estimates can be obtained using this method. Additionally, we establish that the estimated parameters converge normally, extending previous convergence results for the linear Hawkes process. Numerical examples and a real-world application to a dataset of high-frequency financial transactions demonstrate the nonlinear Hawkes process' effectiveness.

Researchers are utilizing linearly polarized lasers with durations between 1-10 ps to generate plasma with densities in the range of 10^17-10^19 cm-3 and create waveplates from plasma, allowing for the adjustment of light polarization rotation rates. Studies have demonstrated that plasma can be made with densities above 10^18 cm-3 and show how the thickness of these waveplates is influenced by magnetic fields and the speed of light, which can be adjusted to vary the polarization rotation over a range of millimeters to meters. These plasma waveplates have applications in enhancing the polarization properties of high-power lasers and their ability to modify polarization properties quickly makes them suitable for lasers with short pulse durations.

We perform an in-depth examination of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment within the Standard Model's two-Higgs doublet extension, specifically type-II. By utilizing a global parameter space, we analyze the potential magnitude of the tau's electric dipole moment mediated by the charged Higgs particles, taking into consideration constraints from the neutral meson mixing phenomena, the $b\rightarrow s\gamma$ process, and the charged lepton flavors' oscillations. By applying numerical methods, we create a 3D map that illustrates the interplay between the tau's electric dipole moment and the charged Higgs parameters, as well as their individual mass spectra. Our study reveals that the tau's electric dipole moment could potentially be substantial, in the range of $10^{-17}$ to $10^{-16}$ e.cm, and may be observable in ongoing and future experiments.

A comprehensive error correction capability analysis is performed for rank metric codes, providing a detailed examination of their decoding capabilities in various metric learning scenarios. The error correction capabilities of rank metric codes are found to behave differently for code rates both above and below 1/2. The paper also presents an alternative construction method for Gabidulin codes, showcasing their capabilities in correcting errors and erasures. Furthermore, the development of an efficient decoding algorithm for a newly defined code type is discussed, which can correct errors and erasures for code rates greater than 1/2. The potential applications of these error correction capabilities in secure distributed matrix data storage and retrieval are also explored.

The unitary conformal field theory on one screen, defined by the AdS$_3$ bulk, contains a wide range of conformal blocks, specifically the geodesic Witten diagrams, which correspond to current conformal partial wave blocks in the near-horizon CFT$_2$. When considering the AdS$_2$ bulk, the same geodesic Witten diagrams exhibit a more complex behavior, with different representations of conformal blocks in the near-horizon CFT$_2$. This distinction in representation can be seen as a manifestation of the difference in boundary conditions in the AdS$_2$ bulk, leading to distinct sets of conformal blocks in the CFT$_2$ on one screen. This phenomenon can be observed across various levels, ranging from individual blocks to the overall structure of the CFT$_2$ and finally to its toroidal universality classes. This distinction also results in a more nuanced understanding of the AdS$_2$ bulk as being composed of two distinct sectors, each corresponding to a specific boundary condition and associated with a unique toroidal universality class of the CFT$_2$ on one screen.

This paper explores the relationship between combinatorial differential manifolds and the f-vectors of simple normal crossing divisors in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Building on the work of Gelfand and MacPherson, it is demonstrated that any combinatorial differential manifolds within $\mathbb{C}^n$ can be represented as a combination of combinatorial subspaces that intersect smoothly. Additionally, it is proven that the number of crossings in these subspaces is limited, leading to a conclusion about the f-vector of any simple normal crossing divisor in $\mathbb{C}^n$. A constructive approach to recovering these subspaces and thereby determining any simple normal crossing divisor in $\mathbb{C}^n$ is also outlined.

The recent observation of the supernova SN~2020jfo, which exhibited unusual elemental abundance patterns, is worth studying. With the aim of examining the chemical changes induced by this event, researchers are analyzing its effects on the surrounding interstellar medium in the Milky Way's center. To better understand the SN~2020jfo's unusual abundance patterns, we are analyzing the element production ratios of nickel to iron, which are crucial for determining the origin of supernovae and the distribution of elements created in the universe. SN~2020jfo's Ni/Fe production ratio is notable for being significantly lower than the solar ratio, a feature more commonly seen in Type Ia supernovae than core-collapse supernovae like SN~2020jfo, which suggests that this event may have additional underlying chemistry.

A lobster-eye optics imaging system divides the space around it into multiple segments based on the speed and image of an object. To analyze a cross-shaped image produced by this system, researchers divide it into four parts using the azimuthal rotation angle. They examine how each part maps to a specific segment of the optics and find that all parts behave differently as the rotation speed changes. To better understand the relationships, a new parameter is introduced that combines the optics' segments and the rotation speed, allowing for further investigation of this unique imaging system.

This study examines a type of fully nonlinear parabolic equation known as a second-order equation, where the unknown function appears in the equation through its level sets. We developed an algorithm based on level set methods to analyze this equation. The algorithm allows us to transform the moving interface problem into a set of partial differential equations with the level set method's standard form. We then proved that our algorithm produces a solution that can be made smooth for any given initial data. Additionally, we showed that it can be used to extend the methods to other types of equations, including fully nonlinear first-order equations and a type of nonlinear second-order Hamilton-Jacobi equation with discontinuous coefficients.

To improve the efficiency of N-body cosmological simulations, a split approach can be employed, where a fast density-only model is used to generate an intermediate grid, and then a lightweight halo finder identifies halos from this grid. However, using this split method in large-scale simulations is computationally expensive due to the required solution of a nonlinear PDE to obtain the halo distribution from the density field. This study bypasses the halo finder by directly solving the non-linear PDE, referred to as the gravity-inversion problem, using machine learning models. We trained two separate neural network architectures, NRAM and RAM, to map the density field to the halo distribution, and halo mass for specific cosmological parameters. Following this, we carried out cosmological simulations with high-resolution simulations, with the goal of identifying $512^3$ halo masses from an existing $1024^3$ density field. We trained and evaluated the effectiveness of NRAM and RAM at predicting halo masses at different scales of initial scalar perturbations, and compared their performance with that of N-body simulations. We discovered that even at very large scales, where halo formation is minimal, a model trained on the halo finder output was more accurate than one trained directly on the N-body simulation data. Additionally, we found that the precision of both models improves with a lower amplitude of initial scalar perturbations, where the NRAM model demonstrated a high level of precision, exceeding $99\%$, when predicting halo masses above $10^{

This study examines the behavior of a rotating, anisotropic star composed of an incompressible fluid, where the angular momentum is evenly distributed among all fluid elements, in contrast to a method where it is assigned to isopycnic surfaces and results in the breakdown of the inverse theorem of the star. By using the method of variations in the time domain, nonlinear evolution equations were derived and then transformed into the laboratory frame of reference. As the star spins faster, the symmetry of axial rotation is broken, resulting in the formation of a prolate oblique mode whose frequency can be calculated based on its definition alone. By comparing calculations for different mass and angular momentum values, additional modes were found to interact and merge into a sequence of non-linearly interacting modes within the star's gravitational field.

This research focuses on developing a cost-effective approach that reduces
data collection expenses for machine learning model training through selective
labeling. To achieve this goal, a convenient source was identified with
potential for providing large amounts of data but is difficult to label, such as
crowdsourcing platforms. To address this challenge, an interesting approach
was taken to label only a small portion of the available data. The challenge
was then framed as a importance sampling non-parametric Bayesian deep
unsupervised learning problem. To solve this problem, a framework was
established that utilized a regularizer to transfer knowledge from labeled data to
unlabeled data. The approach was tested on an image modality change problem
known as selective labeling, where the goal was to label medical images based
on anatomical features. The results showed that even with limited labeling, the
approach was effective in labeling medical images. The method was found to be
effective even when the source and target distributions were different. The
approach was also found to be robust to hyperparameter selection. The challenge
was applied to synthetic medical images called MR-BrainScan, the approach was
able to correctly classify images into different categories with high accuracy
even when the target distribution was significantly different from the source
distribution.

The first observation of the gravitational wave event GW190425 was made in 2019 by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), originating from a binary neutron star merger. New information has become available since the original research, enabling a more in-depth analysis. Our study compares and combines existing data with this fresh insight, exploring the properties of the merged object, neutron star masses, and the amount of heavy element created. Our findings show that this event is more similar to the gamma-ray burst AT2019aeg, occurring immediately after merger, and that the amount of Banja Rees-Mogelberg (r-process) elements produced is comparable to, though possibly less than, that seen in the merger of two neutron stars rather than a neutron star and a black hole.

This research examines the impact of the pandemic's early stages on the diversity of urban encounters and community resilience in one Toronto neighborhood. Combining ethnographic fieldwork with quantitative data from local business surveys, the study reveals a significant decline in diversity within the neighborhood as many non-essential businesses closed or shifted to online-only operations. However, community resilience emerged as residents adapted by increasing interactions with local grocery stores, pharmacies, and food establishments, thus maintaining social connections with a more limited but diverse group of neighbors. The findings demonstrate that even a brief pandemic period can disrupt the long-term features of urban diversity, yet community resilience can be fostered through altered encounters with the local community.

A star surrounded by a disk with gaps and migration features has been found through high-resolution spectroscopy, and further analysis using simulations reveals that large objects within the outer disk could be causing both instability and rapid spin within the inner disk. A recent theoretical study proves that migrating objects in the disk around a young, massive star can create gravitational waves that strengthen the inner disk, battling both the migration and the fragmentation that can occur as the inner disk spins rapidly. Based on current research, it's clear that the behavior of the inner disk around a young, massive star is influenced by both migration and stability within the disk, ultimately leading to the formation of planets.

This study examines the solution methods available for the two-dimensional water wave problem, specifically focusing on the approach that uses the method of characteristics to solve the surface evolution equation, and another that uses the Riemann invariants approach based on the Hamiltonian formulation. A key aspect explored is the solution strategy for recovering the surface elevation from the wave envelope, as well as various numerical methods used to solve the boundary value problem, including the use of the Green's function to solve the Dirichlet problem. A brief overview is also provided of the conditions that define wellposed problems, as well as the approach to solving the Dirichlet problem using the Green's function. A note is made about the relationship between the scalar and vector Green's functions.

This article examines the connection between differential forms and the surface layer theorem in locally convex spaces, revealing that it provides a meaningful context for defining differential forms and shows that they are closely tied to the surface layer theorem. A key discovery revealed by our analysis is that it reinterprets the Cauchy-Riemann equations in these spaces. Additionally, our findings include proving that the space of differential forms is barreled, locally convex, and weakly complete. A detailed exploration of hyperfunction theory through the surface layer theorem and differential forms is also presented.

A layered control framework is introduced for a mobile robot using a sensor module made up of sonar sensors at its base, providing a fast and flexible navigation system.  The dynamic model of the robot's environment is bypassed as the sonar layer produces avoidance commands based solely on distance readings.  As a result, the middle layer, which models the robot's environment, is unnecessary, and the navigation capabilities are enhanced as a result.  The control system was tested in a simulated environment with real-world results showing its effectiveness in navigating complex scenarios with limited sensory input.

It's perceived that news context helps in determining news falsehoods, but until now, there's been limited research on whether utilizing contextual information improves performance when comparing professional fact-checking methods, including machine learning models. Our studies aimed to fill this gap by comparing the accuracy of models utilizing contextual information and identifying factors that influence their effectiveness. Our findings, showing that context significantly enhances the accuracy of models and that utilizing context from multiple sentences yields better results than utilizing context from single sentences, demonstrate that context can be a valuable component in model-based falsehood detection. Additionally, our data indicated that models struggle with titles and headlines, and that the accuracy of models is substantially better when they indicate whether information is true or false rather than providing neutral statements.

In thermodynamic systems undergoing hysteresis, the interplay between driving forces, external parameters, and dynamics results in distinct trajectories on the thermodynamic phase diagram, giving rise to entropy changes and hysteresis. This research investigates a nonlinear optical waveguide, where the curvature effect plays a significant role, and we demonstrate how its impact can lead to the creation of hysteresis and a sudden increase in entropy, marking a critical point. By developing a nonlinear differential equation that takes the curvature into account, we can analyze this phenomenon through a combination of mathematical modeling and numerical methods, revealing the mechanisms driving the curvature-induced phase transitions and nonlinear dynamics. Furthermore, by mapping the solutions to their equivalent form in the Poincar\'e sphere, we can observe the emergence of hysteresis and the beam breakup, which can be related to the polarization dynamics and its impact on the outcome.

This research introduces a two-block formulation and multiple-block variations of the
L1-PCA problem, adapting these formulations to handle outlying data points via the
BRAMA method. The primary contribution of this study lies in its solution strategies
for these optimization problems, which involve developing algorithms for rotationally
invariant L1-PCA with L1-norm and mixed-norm objectives. The proposed method uses
the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to solve these problems, with a
rotational invariance step to address the circular symmetry constraint. Theoretical
results on the convergence rates of the algorithm are also established, with a focus
on solving the two-block formulation. A numerical study is then conducted to compare
the proposed method with other optimization approaches, using both synthetic and
real-world data sets.

Our investigation focuses on improving semantic labeling by leveraging high-quality annotations. In many cases, existing annotated datasets can be repurposed for this goal, but using them directly can be limiting due to the risk of introducing inconsistencies and varying quality control. Our research shows that tasks like paraphrasing can help evaluate the reliability of annotated labels by identifying inconsistencies. In particular, we found that comparing sentence embeddings from labeled data can effectively pinpoint problematic annotations. To take it a step further, we propose a method called Contrastive Correction, which utilizes the reliable annotations to train a model to exclude inconsistent data. When applied to the S2 ORANGE dataset, our approach achieved notable improvements in baseline models, with a significant increase of 4.5% in F1 score. Additionally, our method demonstrated versatility by successfully transferring to new datasets with different characteristics.

Creating accurate 2D maps from mobile agents' trajectories is known as topological mapping.
This technique represents an agent's journey as a series of connected points rather than
a comprehensive global map, which can lead to navigation inefficiencies due to the
absence of positional information.
In response to this limitation, we developed HiTMap, a innovative tracking framework
capable of managing navigation by splitting the process into two stages and
employing a novel 'hub' approach to map construction.
To evaluate HiTMap's effectiveness, we created a simulated environment and a real-world
dataset 'CampusMap'.
In both test cases, our model demonstrated a significant improvement in navigating the
map when compared to current topological mapping methods.

We've determined the limit to which a tiny local magnetic field can be detected using atomic interferometry to be no less than $3.4 \times 10^{-18}$ Tesla, following an experiment that exceeded this limit. This technique involves manipulating atoms in multiple beam interference patterns and measuring the resulting shift caused by the influence of the local magnetic field on the atoms' motion. This method can detect even very slight changes in the frequency of atomic vibrations, allowing for the use of atomic motion frequency as a precise standard of length. This record-breaking detection also marked the first time a local magnetic field was measured in this manner in an atomic experiment featuring entanglement induced by illumination. This experiment occurred at room temperature and utilized a relatively small amount of atoms. A calculation showed that this achievement could be improved by using a more sensitive atomic frequency measurement method known as Ramsey interferometry, to as low as a local magnetic field of $1.5 \times 10^{-20}$ Tesla.

This research investigates the recoverability of admixture weights in models with partially identifiable weights when a Dirichlet process prior is placed on densities. It demonstrates that an excessive increase in the scaling factor of the Dirichlet process prior can result in non-identifiable weights and non-parametric Bayesian mixture inference. It also shows that weights become non-identifiable when the Dirichlet process prior's scaling factor exceeds the number of components, leading to weight recovery being equivalent to uniform sampling from the Dirichlet distribution. Furthermore, it shows under certain conditions that with a large enough Dirichlet process prior scaling factor, the admixture distribution converges to a Dirichlet process itself, allowing for the inference of the Dirichlet process prior from data. It also provides a method for inferring the admixture weights and the Dirichlet process prior's scaling factor, and demonstrates the effectiveness of this method using synthetic and real-world data.

As homogenous GPU architectures have given way to specialized accelerators like
Tensor Cores and Vector Engines, programming these devices has become increasingly
complicated. Memory management on these GPUs is particularly difficult due to
limited global memory access and varying block sizes. In response to these
challenges, a wide range of specialized memory allocators has been developed for
GPU programming, each attempting to optimize performance for different applications
by allocating memory in large blocks. However, these allocators often result in
memory waste and performance slowdowns, especially for applications with dynamic
memory requirements. In an effort to address this issue, a new memory allocator
known as DynaSOAr has been created, one that dynamically adjusts block sizes to
minimize memory fragmentation while exceeding traditional memory allocator performance
benchmarks. By comparing DynaSOAr to leading memory allocators, including Nsight,
CUDA's built-in memory allocator, tests have shown that DynaSOAr achieves
significantly faster execution times and lower memory usage on real-world accelerators.

Recently, the concept of magnetic atomic doublets has been reevaluated due to the precise control over spin-orbit coupling in two-dimensional materials. Theoretical studies have typically considered small ensembles of adatoms or a single adatom in isolation. However, in real-world scenarios, it's common to find both individual and paired magnetic atomic doublets in proximity to each other and with varying distances between them. This study examines the local density of states near paired magnetic atomic doublets in graphene and hBN using a multi-atomic model under non-equilibrium conditions. Our findings show that the spin-paired states' peak positions shift significantly due to spin-orbit coupling, resulting in the splitting of states in the presence of paired atomic doublets. Our data also reveal that the spin-orbit coupling's effect can be either positive, zero, or negative, depending on the inter-atomic distance and the environment. Experimental verification of these predictions is feasible using in-situ techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy, and our results provide a basis for interpreting such data.

Recently discovered transiting mini-Neptunes in a star system are found to orbit close to the habitable zone of their star. We studied 24 exoplanet candidates that orbited small, cool stars within the TESS database's first data set and found four planets with sizes less than 3.5 times that of Jupiter that likely pass in front of their star. Using statistical methods to account for factors like planet multiplicity and stellar evolution, we found that these four planets likely have semi-major axes within 1.5 astronomical units of their stars and could potentially support life on their surfaces.

We used theoretical modeling to examine the substitutional and interstitial sites in rutile TiO2 for carbon and nitrogen atoms. Calculations were performed using the screened exchange plus U method to account for localization, and we found that in both substitutional and interstitial positions, the atoms exhibit a tendency for covalent bonding with their surroundings. When substituted or located in interstitial sites, C and N atoms display similar tendencies in their physical properties, differing significantly from their counterparts in bulk C and N materials. Both substitutional and interstitial C and N atoms in TiO2 present a mix of $sp^2$ and $p$ orbital characteristics, and all cases show a direct covalent bond between the atoms and their oxygen neighbors. We also observed that both substitutional and interstitial C and N atoms in TiO2 possess a positive bond center (BC) energy, indicating stability within the lattice.

Our research involves an examination of the production of long-lived neutral particles at the LHC using the ATLAS detector, specifically within the context of semi-elastic processes involving top quarks and top antiquarks that decay into $W$ bosons and top quarks/antiquarks, respectively. By applying various requirements, we narrow down our dataset to feature events with two forward jets, missing transverse energy, and one isolated lepton, resulting in the establishment of lower limits on the likelihood of certain quark decays that violate the conservation of fundamental symmetries. These limits range from $3.1\times 10^{-4}$ (at 95% certainty) for decays occurring in $O(10^9)$ GeV-scale particles with short lifetimes, to lower limits of $2.5\times 10^{-3}$ (at 95% certainty) for decays taking place in particles with medium lifetimes, and a limit of $1.6\times 10^{-3}$ (at 95% certainty) for those with long lifetimes.

Consider the task of partitioning the edges of a given graph into different color groups based on the lengths of their paths in another graph, while ensuring no edges within the same group are connected by a path of a certain length in the second graph. A recent study proved that any triangle-edge coloring of a graph can result in a specific color distribution, and this was previously done for specific types of triangles in earlier works. The current study shows that any triangle-edge coloring of a graph can adhere to a particular distribution, provided the graph meets certain conditions and has a specific property called high 'cover' density. The study also provides an updated lower bound for triangle-edge coloring under certain conditions. The current study further explores methods to combine multiple graphs that can achieve a particular color distribution. The key findings include an algorithm for creating a particular color distribution based on the union of two graphs, a general approach for combining multiple graphs to achieve the same effect, and a notable application for directed trees. The study on triangle-edge coloring also offers a significant improvement over an earlier bound established by the same authors in a previous work. The approach presented in this study offers an interesting edge-coloring problem and a potential solution strategy that may be useful for other related problems.

Quantum systems, whether qubits or qutrits, are susceptible to degradation due to surrounding noise during measurements, which can be measured using quantum non-orthogonality. As a qutrit-based coherent hedgehog gravitationally masses a qutrit particle, we examine how noise affects this system under both free fall and rotation conditions. Comparing qutrits and qubits of equal complexity, we find that qutrits are more resistant to noise affecting their gravitational mass, while both qutrits and qubits exhibit similar sensitivity to noise affecting their non-orthogonality. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the minimal number of error corrections required to maintain a reliable mass measurement is directly proportional to the number of qutrit levels and is independent of the gravitational environment.

The polarization of a beam must be extremely high in certain particle physics applications, including the generation of polarized positron beams in experiments like Belle II and the PANDA experiment at the FAIR facility. To achieve the desired polarization levels, a method is proposed to use laser-intersted polarization modulation in electron-positron storage rings, based on a concept previously tested at the SLC storage ring at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. Using this technique, researchers aim to exceed a polarization threshold of 30% in positrons and demonstrate the feasibility of this method for future high-polarization experiments. At the Stanford Linear Collider, a beam spin rotation of approximately 45 degrees was achieved in a 50 GeV positron beam through a 1 mm diameter interaction region, allowing for a comparison with theoretical models and the potential for application to the PANDA experiment at the FAIR facility in Darmstadt, Germany.
We establish that finite groups exhibiting polynomial diameter growth also have a limited number of conjugacy classes that scale polynomially and do not contain infinite nilpotent subgroups.

A novel, ultra-low-power temperature sensor has been developed using a
sub-threshold 65nm CMOS process. This sensor can operate at 300K and measure
temperature across the 300-340K range with an inaccuracy of 1.5°C. With a
supply voltage of 300mV, the sensor achieves a conversion time of 10.6ms and
a root mean square error of 0.45°C without calibration. When operating at
325K, the sensor consumes an average power of 0.13μW, making it suitable for
battery-powered applications in areas with extreme temperatures.

This article provides a detailed explanation of the concept of topological groupoid extensions and their equivalence to gerbes over topological stacks. We establish a connection between these notions by utilizing the framework of local inertia groups. We also introduce the fundamental groupoid of a topological stack and demonstrate that it leads to a sequence analogous to that found in the classical context of the fundamental group. Furthermore, we show that the fundamental groupoid of a line bundle gerbe over a line obtains a groupoid structure isomorphic to its monodromy group.

A statistical analysis of molecular cores was performed to investigate the relationship between their mass growth and the formation of massive stars. Located in the Carina cloud, these cores were selected based on their similarity to massive star-forming cores and were compared to cores that had formed massive stars and had surrounding outflows and H II regions. Both core groups demonstrated similar mass growth rates and were driven by the accretion of solid material from the cloud. As a result, neither core was found to have stars formed within it, suggesting that the transition from core to massive star formation may be complex and influenced by factors other than mass.

This research examines the impact of applying differentiation and integration operators from classical calculus to positive definite zonal functions. It demonstrates that these operations result in functions that are positive definite within specific function classes, including harmonic polynomials and special Hermite polynomials. Additionally, it provides a theoretical framework for defining differentiation and integration operators for zonal functions and shows that these operators have the desired effect of producing positive definite functions. It also provides concrete examples by applying these concepts to specific functions, such as harmonic polynomials and the Schur function.

The model foam's rheology is described by a relatively simple equation that accounts for the effects of two key parameters: the surface-to-volume ratio and the distance between plateaus in the stress-strain curve. Based on this equation, the surface-to-volume ratio can be inferred from the stress-relaxation curve, especially when the model includes the effects of plateau radius and plateaus' distribution. The calculated surface-to-volume ratios match the physically measured values in laboratory experiments, demonstrating that the model effectively captures the interplay between geometry and rheology in model foams. Stress-relaxation curves from the model and experimental data show a strong agreement, with a coefficient of determination (R-squared) value of 0.93 for one set of data and 0.90 for another.

Ensemble methods for combining different deep learning models have shown significant performance improvements in various computer vision tasks.  In our research, ensemble classifiers were successfully applied to enhance the performance of convolutional neural networks in image classification.  We achieved notable improvements by combining different models, including a single wide residual network and multi-task training with language models.  Our findings were validated through multiple experiments, revealing that ensemble classifiers consistently outperformed the individual models.  Our approach has been demonstrated to be a straightforward and effective technique for boosting the performance of existing deep learning models in various vision tasks.

A rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a membrane separating two fluids is studied as it experiences stress and strain, and the role of tension in the membrane is examined, particularly how it affects the stability of various states, such as rotation-driven circulation, circulation driven by surface tension, and stationary states, through linear analysis and numerical solutions. The research reveals that the membrane's tension can cause circulation to become unstable at very low rotation rates and that surface-tension-driven circulation can coexist with rotation-driven circulation only when the difference in pressure driven by the two forces is significant, and this coexistence can lead to a pattern of rolling vortices.

An examination of the cyano and chloro derivatives of cyclopentadiene and
benzene is provided, with a focus on comparing their abundance ratios. These
species were created through the reaction of CCH and CN radicals with C$_5$H
$_5$ and C$_6$H$_6$ respectively, and also with CCl$_2$ and CBr$_2$ to
produce corresponding chloro and bromo derivatives. An astronomical context
for these findings is provided by comparing their abundance ratios seen in the
interstellar medium, specifically in the TMC-1 protostar, with ratios of
96:1 and 1383:1 for CCH/CN and CN/CCCH$_2$ respectively, and 254:1 for
CBr$_3$/CBrN and 48:1 for CBrN/CCBr$_2$.

Neural machine translation models have significantly improved in recent years, thanks in large part to the development of attention-based models.  However, these models suffer from a limitation in understanding the context of future tokens in the target sentence due to their sequential nature.  To address this limitation, we introduce a look-ahead attention mechanism that allows the model to consider the context of specific future tokens, which can be either arbitrary or constrained by a reinforcement learning signal.  We further explore two variants of the look-ahead attention mechanism: one that attends to the most suitable future token and another that distributes the attention across a subset of future tokens.  Our experiments on the English-to-German translation task demonstrate a substantial improvement in translating rare words and a notable gain in translating technical texts, measured by the BLEU score.

The technical development of grid computing is facing challenges in translating its concepts, models, architectures, protocols, and technologies into practical reality. To address this issue, this paper employs a translational architecture for grid computing, which includes source, process, product layers to explore the semantics and dynamics of grid computing from various perspectives. By analyzing the trust relationships between grid agents, this paper further delves into the details of a scheme for secure data sharing and storage in grid computing.

The cosmological expansion history can be reinterpreted using the Einstein gravity framework in terms of modifications to the stress-energy tensor through a time-varying viscosity coefficient. The effect of this viscous coefficient on the evolution of the universe has been observed in several studies using observational data from supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations. In this research, we used a parametric approach to model the viscosity coefficient as a function of the universe's energy density, applying it to three distinct observational datasets. We then compared the corresponding model simulations to observational data sets, including supernovae, the cosmic microwave background from the CMB, and various scales of the universe, in order to determine the values of model parameters. The findings were then used to determine the current and future evolution of the universe, with the result that the Einstein gravity framework, characterized by a positive and increasing viscosity coefficient, aligns with the observed data, revealing a closed and eventually expanding universe scenario.

Using an advanced machine learning approach, The LHC Dark Matter Working Group has performed an in-depth re-analysis of J/	au 	o 	invisible decay data from four major LHC experiments. By applying a decay width upper limit of 1 nb, and considering the J/	au 	production cross section at 8 TeV, limits on dark matter properties have been established. For a dark matter mediator mass below 600 GeV, the effective scalar dark matrix coupling divided by the nucleon dark matter scattering cross section can be as low as 1.6 x 10^-6, based on existing limits. However, when considering a vector mediator, effective couplings below 3.4 x 10^-5 can be excluded for masses up to 800 GeV, and nucleon-scattering cross sections below 8.6 x 10^-48 GeV^-2 for masses below 600 GeV. These results demonstrate the significance of J/	au 	invisible decay data in constraining dark matter models.

Deep learning techniques, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks, have effectively addressed multi-field statistical similarity assessment, enabling widespread practical applications, such as analyzing temperature curves and remote sensing images. This study extends the similarity assessment to a comprehensive framework incorporating multiple features, similar to Convolutional Neural Networks, and designates it the Multi-Feature Similarity Assessment. This assessment assesses the similarity between two images by calculating a score, and can be applied to various contexts, including image compression, editing, and manipulation. This study also introduces a comprehensive evaluation dataset for multi-feature similarity assessment, consisting of 5000 pairs of natural images. Experimental results on this dataset demonstrate that the proposed assessment method is highly effective in predicting the similarity score, with a ranking accuracy of 73.4% in ranking the similarity pairs and a mean absolute error of 0.34 in predicting the similarity score. Furthermore, the proposed assessment method is compared with existing similarity metrics, including VGG and AlexNet-based assessments, showing its superiority over these methods.

This research examines the asymptotic characteristics of a random walk with independently identically distributed (i.i.d.) zero-mean increments, and it analyzes how the scaling parameter 'b' influences these characteristics. If the scaling factor 'b' grows in a specific way, we demonstrate that the asymptotic distribution of the random walk can be either normal or stable, depending on whether the characteristic function of a single step is weakly mixing or non-trivial. If 'b' does not adhere to this growth pattern, we show that the asymptotic distribution will be neither normal nor stable. Additionally, we establish lower and upper bounds for the moments of large deviations of the random walk.

This research examined the relationship between plasma parameters, including
temperature and density, and the functioning of plasma sources. Combining an
analytical ODE model with an optimization algorithm led to the development
of an optimal control strategy for plasma sources. By adjusting input power
levels, this approach aimed to achieve desired plasma conditions. The proposed
methodology was applied to three distinct plasma source models, each
demonstrating the capacity to achieve optimized plasma parameters. The key
features and theoretical foundations of the source models in question are outlined in the accompanying document.

This paper introduces a novel W-shaped network to achieve high precision and efficiency in detecting and outlining nuclear regions in cytological images. To improve performance, the W-shaped network was designed to combine multi-scale feature extraction and refining processes, using both atrous spatial decomposition and standard convolution layers in its current configuration. To further enhance results, a modified U-shaped sub-network was developed to accurately outline nuclear regions and train the model using a combined loss function. The proposed approach was tested and showed significant performance enhancements over conventional U-shaped networks and other state-of-the-art methods, achieving average precision rates of 0.83, 0.86, and 0.91 for respectively small, medium, and large nuclear regions.

We derive the rank of twists for local gamma factors for the odd special orthogonal group and the symplectic group from specific isomorphism properties of representations. This analysis leads to the evidence that the rank of twists for the even special orthogonal group can be determined by the rank of twists for the symplectic group and the odd special orthogonal group, considering the local factors of gamma.

To gain insight into Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), we examine their fundamental connection to conventional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks. By interpreting GCNs through the lens of their equivalent form using graph theory, we demonstrate how the graph convolution operation resembles a path-based generalization of local spatial operations found in traditional CNNs and Neural Networks. Our analysis reveals that the impact of the graph convolution operation is directly related to the features of the graph, specifically how it affects node representations in GCNs. Our approach to examining GCNs through the prism of traditional networks is confirmed to yield comparable performance in various benchmark tasks, according to our experimental results.

This study examines the entropy of rotating black holes within Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity, focusing on the case with a non-trivial 'hair'. The analysis reveals that the entropy of these solutions falls short of the entropy of vacuum Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity for pure gravity. The research also compares the entropy of the rotating solutions in Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity with the entropy of the corresponding solutions in $N=8$ supergravity in $4$-dimensional space-time. The findings demonstrate that the entropy of the solutions in $N=8$ supergravity exceeds that of the Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity in a specific ratio, with the same scaling behavior for both rotating and static solutions. The research further explores the implications for the 'hairy' black hole proposal and the membrane paradigm in Chern-Simons theory. The study also calculates the entropy of rotating solutions in Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity with a non-trivial dilaton field, discovering that the entropy remains sub-lattice, albeit with a modified scaling factor. The research also examines the solutions with a non-trivial axion field, finding that they lack 'hair', and compares the entropy of the solutions with the corresponding $N=8$ supergravity in a specific sub-lattice scaling scenario.

This study investigates the challenges faced by ultrasound elastography, specifically the difficulties encountered in estimating axial and lateral tissue displacements caused by sound wave interactions with tissue. Axial displacement estimation is generally considered more accurate than lateral estimation due to the distinct endocardial reflection that can be used as a reference point, allowing for more reliable strain calculations. However, determining the speed of sound in tissue is essential for accurately calculating lateral displacements, which can be difficult to achieve in ultrasound elastography due to incomplete information about the speed of sound in tissue. An alternative approach presented in this research uses beamforming to measure the time delay between the initial pulse and the return signal, which is then used to estimate the speed of sound in tissue, necessary for accurately calculating lateral displacements.

This paper introduces two new specifications: FLC and FS for methods that manipulate sets, defining their behavior using formal logical pseudocodes that adhere to precise rules to prevent errors and ensure safety. We demonstrate how these specifications can be used to analyze the correctness and safety of methods that operate on sets, even after modifications have been made. A key aspect of these specifications is that they are non-executable, unlike traditional pseudocodes, and are instead descriptive of intended behavior. We show that these non-executable pseudocodes can be effectively used to verify the correctness and safety of methods through testing, without the need for formal verification. We also introduce a new testing approach that leverages additional test data to ensure that tests accurately reflect the intended behavior of the methods being tested. This approach enables efficient testing of methods against their intended behavior, ensuring that tests are both correct and safe. We demonstrate the efficiency of this approach through a comparative analysis of random testing, flaky testing, and our proposed method, which includes both theoretical time complexity comparisons and a practical experiment using method signatures from the Apache Commons Collections library.

This paper presents a first-ever algorithm that creates a coreset for the $k$-means clustering issue, completing the theoretical foundation established by Porat in 2015. Unlike previous methods, this one-time pass algorithm generates a coreset with an optimal size of $O(k^2 \cdot d)$ for data points in a $d$-dimensional space, making it the first to achieve optimal scaling in the number of clusters for real-valued input data. The duration of this coreset construction process is directly proportional to the input size, making it efficient for large datasets. The coreset produced by this approach can be used in various applications, including an optimized $k$-means clustering algorithm and approximate data matching queries. The key steps and properties of the coreset construction process are demonstrated through extensive experiments. The techniques introduced in this research, such as the use of flat clusters and multiple levels of coreset creation, provide valuable insights that can be applied to various coreset-related problems. The open-source code for this project is available on GitHub.

In large-scale grid worlds, an agent can divide the environment into distinct areas, dubbed "superstates," to simplify navigation and decision-making. By applying this strategy, known as state-partitioning, the agent can efficiently navigate to specific locations while avoiding obstacles and navigating complex paths. This research explores two new applications for state-partitioning: one where an agent must evade multiple pursuers, and another where the agent must navigate through a maze while avoiding being misled by incorrect path information. To solve these problems, a novel method called Dynamic Grid Discretization is proposed, which allows the agent to dynamically divide the grid based on probability distributions. This approach yields better results than existing methods that use pre-defined grids, especially in scenarios with dynamic and uncertain environments.

A recent development involves the identification of universal corrections to W and Z PDFs resulting from QCD interactions. This phenomenon has been mathematically represented as an enhancement to the standard DGLAP evolution equations and has been verified through numerical means using commonly utilized PDF sets. Our research extends previous findings by demonstrating that these corrections make significant contributions at TeV-scale colliders, specifically in the high-mass W and Z boson production regions. Our key contributions include developing an improved PDF reweighting method that can account for these corrections within PDF sets derived from global data, in addition to verifying that these methods are effective in various contexts through a range of theoretical and experimental checks. We also demonstrate the relevance of these findings to current and future experiments at the LHC.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a single dynamics model that learns from across multiple tasks has both benefits and drawbacks. On the one hand, it can facilitate efficient transfer by leveraging similarities in dynamics across different tasks. However, it may also lead to overfitting or the model prioritizing common dynamics over task-specific ones, potentially hindering performance in individual tasks. We introduce Multi-Dynamics Proximal Policy Optimization (MD-PPO), a method that capitalizes on multiple learned dynamics models to discover the most beneficial dynamics for each task by accounting for differences in value functions. We explore various model ensemble strategies and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in both simulated and real-world environments, showing that using multiple dynamics models can yield improved performance compared to using a single model, and that our MD-PPO algorithm outperforms alternative ensemble methods and baselines in a variety of settings.

We derive a new form of Godel's second incompleteness theorem from Godel's first incompleteness theorem and demonstrate that it is essentially equivalent to a recently enhanced version by Rosser, which indicates that a formal system cannot prove the consistency of itself is a more robust restatement of the second incompleteness theorem. This is achieved by utilizing a more fundamental approach based on the principles of provability, without relying on transfinite induction in the construction of the fixed point. This methodical proof of the second incompleteness theorem through the first incompleteness theorem offers a distinct, self-sufficient proof of both the theorems.

This paper provides an extension of Hadamard's three circles theorem to real-valued functions in higher dimensions, incorporating the use of Dirac operators. Specifically, it proves that a function f is harmonic if Riemann's integral formula holds for three circles in n dimensions, and demonstrates that this results simplifies to a version of Hadamard's three circles theorem in these dimensions. Additionally, it shows that this outcome can be further generalized to a higher dimensional context, where the focus is on real-valued functions that are monogenic with respect to the Clark operator in the Lorentzian space R0n+1.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning model, the regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN (RCWGAN), to efficiently produce posterior samples in image processing tasks, such as MRI image reconstruction and compressed sensing. The RCWGAN model effectively generates synthetic posteroirs by minimizing the conditional Wasserstein distance between synthetic and target posterior distributions. However, training this model is complicated due to non-differentiable terms in the Wasserstein distance, which can be mitigated by using the Sinkhorn algorithm. To further improve sample generation, the RCWGAN model incorporates an entropy term to promote the diversity of posterior samples. Theoretical assessments and empirical evaluations demonstrate that the RCWGAN model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both diversity and accuracy of generated posterior samples. The code for this project can be found at: \url{https://github.com/zhongyuyu1995/RCWGAN}.

This research paper examines the concepts of invariance and positive invariance for linear subspaces within fractional order systems. We derive conditions for a linear subspace to be considered invariant to a fractional order system, and then extend these principles to define positive invariance. These results are demonstrated to maintain their validity in the presence of time-varying coefficients. We also develop methods for identifying the smallest positively invariant linear subspace and prove these techniques to be effective.

Observations of the 39.5-year radio pulse stream from the neutron star, PSR B1133+16, made over 30 years, were analyzed to reconstruct its surrounding interstellar medium. A comprehensive model was developed to decompose the signal and reveal the hidden structure, recovering each individual scattering screen along the pulse propagation path to Earth, approximately 8 light-years long. The data resolution was sufficient to distinguish reflections from 15 separate screens, revealing a gradient in density gradients across the line of sight, a characteristic not previously observed around this star. The scattering data were combined with observations of the pulse width and polarization, yielding precise measurements of the star's rotation period, pulse emission latitude, the age of the star, the rate of pulsar wind nebulae, and the number of visible scintles, offering insights into the long-distance environment and the physics of pulsar winds.

Deep neural network structures with cascaded layers have demonstrated superior performance in modeling speech signals with periodic patterns, due in part to their ability to dynamically adjust sample sizes. This technique has been applied in speech processing tasks such as denoising, as well as in modeling periodic patterns in other applications. While previous research has focused on designing better cascade block architectures, little attention has been given to understanding the underlying dynamics of sample sizes in periodic signals. This paper explores this issue with an eye on improving the efficiency of sample sizes in cascaded networks. We introduce a new dynamic sample size change model inspired by the linear repetition time (LRT) feature of speech signals, and combine it with a cascade network to create a more streamlined model. This approach results in a reduced sample size that aligns with real-world data, and results in a 4 times decrease in the sample size required for accurate speech separation.

This involves demonstrating that THH lifts from the realm of bicategories to bicategoricals within the 2-cat framework, and that this extension results in a natural correspondence with shadows. Furthermore, we determine that the cyclotomic structure on the 2-cat ∞-category of (∞,2)-algebras is equivalent to the THH-induced structure on the 2-cat ∞-category of bicategories. This is coupled with the observation that THH lifts from the 2-cat framework to the 3-cat framework of tricategories, resulting in a correspondence with shadows within the 3-cat framework, and showing that this correspondence respects the cyclotomic structure.

This study introduces the Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), a novel model that operates within the Poincaré ball to identify high-dimensional manifold graphs. Unlike existing hyperbolic GCNs, LGCN successfully applies graph convolution on Lorentzian manifolds without relying on the Euclidean metric, thus allowing for more generalizations to Spacetime GCNs. We prove that LGCN can capture node features on Lorentzian manifolds and demonstrate its superiority over current hyperbolic GCNs by comparing results of node feature representations. Additionally, LGCN surpasses existing methods in classification tasks on graph datasets generated within the Poincaré ball.

This study focuses on the stability of solutions to the inverse problem of determining the potential of a Schrödinger equation in a periodic setting, using a single measurement of the wave function. Uniqueness proof for the problem is based on an observability inequality, and stability results are derived from an optimal version of an observability inequality and a uniqueness proof from a single measurement. A strategy is proposed to numerically solve the problem using a hybrid method combining a low-resolution optimization problem with a high-resolution solver, and a simple experimental setup is proposed to test the approach.

A statistical distribution known as the Tsallis distribution was initially proposed in 1988 to describe systems that defy the conventional expectation of equal probability distributions. However, the Tsallis distribution's significance was largely misunderstood or misinterpreted for many years. This study aims to demonstrate that the Tsallis distribution can be viewed as a product of independent components, consistent with the concept of 'independent systems,' which is a fundamental principle in social network analysis. As a result, the apparent paradox of the Tsallis distribution can be resolved, revealing its statistical properties that align with those of social systems composed of multiple, independent components. The study also provides a renormalization approach to obtain the Tsallis distribution and applies it to analyze real-world data from Twitter posts.

This article examines the general linearized gravity theory, incorporating a mass term for gravitational perturbations, within a de Sitter expansion. The inclusion of a mass term causes the degrees of freedom to change as the scale parameter shifts, resulting in the conversion of a scalar degree of freedom to a coupled degree of freedom and the creation of a new decoupled degree of freedom. The article also investigates the inclusion of a Chern-Simons term in order to prevent the formation of a tachyonic state in time-like gradients. The research is carried out within a gradient expansion in a de Sitter setting, utilizing a transverse-helicity basis for perturbations and a tHooft's mass parameter parameterization. The analysis reveals that the inclusion of a mass term or a Chern-Simons term in linearized gravity results in an alteration of the degrees of freedom in a way that depends on the scale parameter. The findings in the article also apply to an anti-de Sitter setting, such as in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence theory where the role of the Chern-Simons term is performed by boundary terms.

A mathematical framework for evaluating expectation values of Hamiltonian dynamics is developed, refining previous work by Schrader and Pielawski. This framework includes four types of quantum equilibrium states: (1) those resulting from time-evolution, (2) periodic states, (3) states with multiple equilibrium states, and (4) ratchet states. A key aspect of this framework is the introduction of a quantum Wigner function, allowing the calculation of quantum expectation values. This framework is applied to closed and open quantum systems, ultimately leading to a stochastic dynamics scenario.

A simple quantum harmonic oscillator model is proposed as a two-level system, where energy levels are represented by the ground and excited states. We illustrate how negative temperature can manifest in this model, by applying it to the specific scenario of thermal equilibrium between the oscillator and a heat bath of radiation. We then derive the conditions under which the oscillator's temperature could take on a negative value, assuming its initial temperature is non-zero and its interaction with the bath is stronger than its energy spacing. We also derive the solution for the population inversion, as well as the oscillator's average energy, in the negative temperature state. We further discuss the requirements for a system to exhibit a negative temperature, using the oscillator and its interaction with the radiation as an example. We also derive the equation that describes the change in population inversion over time, using a decay parameter that characterizes the system's non-equilibrium behavior. We then discuss the distinction between the inverse temperature and the parameter that measures the deviation from equilibrium in a non-equilibrium open system. We also discuss how the oscillator's population inversion and average energy can become complex quantities in the case of a driven system. We also derive the equation that describes the time-dependent average energy in a driven system, assuming a constant driving force and decay. This research investigates a type of minimal dark sector that incorporates a dark parity symmetry, known as the "dark minimal left-right symmetry," and applies it to explain the mass origins of dark matter and dark neutrinos. By integrating the dark sector with the standard model, a non-zero neutrino mass is achieved through the "seesaw mechanism." The research demonstrates that the vacuum stability constraints all neutrino masses to be negative, and all dark neutrino masses must observe the "normal hierarchy." Additionally, the research reveals that the dark neutrino sector can exhibit either "dark left-right symmetry" or "inverted mass hierarchy," depending on the mass matrix structure. The research also presents the allowed parameter ranges for the dark neutrinos and the dark gluon, and it proposes the "dark left-right symmetry" as a potential explanation for the observed positron excess of the cosmic ray.

To understand the underlying physics of transition metal oxides, it's crucial to grasp the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) at play. However, measuring SOC directly can be challenging due to interactions and crystal field splitting complicating the energy levels. A theoretical model is developed to extract the impact of SOC from the energy spectra of two-dimensional (2D) transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers after accounting for localizing effects and crystal field splitting. Using in-situ angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), researchers measured the energy levels of Mo and W-based 2D monolayers with different d-orbital occupancies. The analysis of these energy levels reveals the influence of SOC on the band structure, revealing a stronger SOC in W-based 2D monolayers (0.43 eV) compared to Mo-based ones (0.35 eV). The effective SOC also explains the ferromagnetic ordering observed in W-based 2D monolayers. The method presented can be applied to other transition metal oxides to uncover the fundamental physics governing these materials.

In this study, we establish a connection between the relative $I$-functions of a specific class of algebraic varieties and the Gamma functions of multiple Euler integrals. Toric complete intersections with smooth divisors are the focus of our analysis. We demonstrate that given two varieties within this class that share the same underlying lattice, their relative $I$-functions are in a multiplicative relationship, similar to the properties of the Gamma functions associated with multiple Euler integrals. Furthermore, we show that the relative $I$-functions of three varieties that form a chain (i.e., the relative of the first with respect to the second is equivalent to the relative of the second with respect to the third) are invariant under composition. As a consequence, we derive that the relative $I$-functions of varieties with a common underlying lattice form an abelian monoid.

A significant issue with generative medical models is their failure to
develop representations that can be modified to alter the depiction of medical
conditions within the images. Our proposed model, MedEdit, successfully
incorporates guidance from the diagnosis to direct the generative process and
accurately represents the findings from medical imaging modalities such as
MRI and X-ray. When trained on standalone images, MedEdit images show a
considerable improvement in quality, achieving state levels in evaluation
metrics. When guided by the diagnosis, MedEdit accurately generates altered
images
that match the medical condition's new description, achieving high levels of
accuracy in assessment. Our model's capabilities have been demonstrated across
four different medical imaging datasets. Our code has been made available at
the address https://github.com/ghassen-oueda/MedEdit.

In the current digital age, people encounter vast amounts of data regularly, and it's common for this data to exist in a high-dimensional space. Effective visualization techniques are crucial for interpreting such data. A novel application of a cell decomposition method called Pythagorean triples is utilized to depict high-dimensional data points on a two-dimensional map by preserving the distances between points. This approach has been put into practice through the creation of an user-friendly tool called ViDaExpert, designed to easily visualize and explore high-dimensional data. ViDaExpert has already been utilized in visualizing data related to research in astronomy and has the potential to be useful in a wide range of other fields that involve the study of high-dimensional data.
